result.summary: Pausanias finishes the Heraclid kings of Argos, noting how the Argives cut royal power down. He then describes the temple of Lycian Apollo at Argos, its founding by Danaus after a wolf and bull omen, and the statues and tombs around it.

scenes.title: Decline of the Argive kings
scenes.summary: Temenus favours Deiphontes and is killed by his sons. The Argives then reduce the kings' power until Meltas is deposed.
scenes.stakes: Temenus risks his life by favouring his son-in-law over his sons.

scenes.title: Danaus and the wolf omen
scenes.summary: Danaus and Gelanor compete for the kingdom. A wolf defeats a bull, and the Argives read it as a sign for Danaus, who builds the temple.
scenes.stakes: Danaus and Gelanor compete for the kingship of Argos.

scenes.title: Temple contents and monuments
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists the statues, the fire of Phoroneus, Hypermnestra's offering, tombs and altars near the temple.
scenes.stakes: Hypermnestra was tried by her father for disobeying him.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet meaning Wolf-God, linked here to the wolf omen.

notable_quotes.reason: Argives deny Prometheus gave fire, crediting Phoroneus instead.

analysis.text: The chapter links kingship and religion: an omen decides the throne and a temple commemorates it.
The Argives' fondness for equality and the erosion of kingship reflects Argos's move to a civic polity.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias remarks that early statues were all wooden, especially Egyptian ones.

language_notes.text: Temenus, Cresphontes and the sons of Aristodemus were the Heraclid (descendants of Hercules) leaders who shared the Peloponnese after the Dorian conquest.
"Home rule" means self-government by the citizens themselves, rather than rule by a monarch; "left the royal title only" means kings kept the name without real power.
"Lycian" is linked by Pausanias to the Greek word for wolf, lykos; hence the gloss "Wolf-God". Ancient writers also connected it to Lycia.
"Ingratiating words" are flattering, favour-seeking speeches meant to win the people's goodwill.
Nemea, in the Argolid, hosted the Nemean Games and a famous sanctuary of Zeus; Biton's feat was thus tied to a major Argive festival.
Prometheus is the Titan who in common myth stole fire for mankind; the Argives claim their own hero Phoroneus discovered it instead.
Danaus ordered his fifty daughters to kill their cousins, the sons of Aegyptus, on their wedding night. Hypermnestra spared her husband Lynceus.
The bull-and-wolf fight refers to the Argive legend of Danaus and Gelanor, where a wolf defeating a bull was read as an omen for Danaus.
Linus is a legendary early poet and musician, said to be killed by Apollo; Psamathe, his mother in Argive tradition, was Crotopus' daughter.
This refers to the Seven against Thebes, who marched to restore Polynices to the city; the oath bound them to die if they failed.
The Opuntians, from Opus in Locris, also claimed to hold Prometheus' tomb, so the two claims compete.

context_notes.text: Meltas was the last Argive king; after his deposition Argos became a government without kings.
Attalus is the Athenian sculptor who made the temple's statue in Pausanias' time; Danaus's wooden image was the original offering.
Danaus was a legendary Egyptian prince who fled to Argos with his fifty daughters, and claimed rule there.
Epeus is the Greek who built the Trojan Horse in legend; statues attributed to him are ancient wooden images.
Ladas was a celebrated runner, said to have won the long foot race at Olympia. Hermes was credited with inventing the lyre from a tortoise shell.

literary_notes.text: Temenus's favouritism toward his daughter and son-in-law brings about his own death at the hands of his sons.
The wolf and bull stand for the rival men; the wolf's wildness mirrors Danaus the outsider, the bull the native, established Gelanor.
The animal fight is read as predicting the political contest's outcome, a typical omen story in which nature signals the result.
Danaus's motives, self-protection and shame at being outshone, show him as a cruel, self-interested ruler rather than a just father.
Pausanias openly weighs rival local claims and states his own skepticism, giving the guide-book a critical, personal tone.
